Relays (pre-registered, brain only; the 13 Oct headline and 15 Oct lines unchanged): 23 Oct: our earlier controls matched each relay neuron's activity, but not how strongly it connects to the turn neuron. This time the control is a group of other active neurons that excite the turn neuron, chosen so that together they fire about as much as the active relays and send about as many synapses to the turn neuron (both within 20%). Left eye: in 1 of 5 matched groups the turn neuron's rate fell as low as, or lower than, with the relays silenced (matched groups 13-31 Hz, relays 16.0 Hz, nothing silenced 21-25 Hz). By our pre-registered rule, this test does not show that the relays matter more than other inputs with the same combined connection strength and activity. Right eye: among the 9 other active neurons that excite the turn neuron, no group came within 20% of the relays on both combined activity and synapse count (we had set 5 groups as the minimum in advance), so this control could not be built for this eye. Our rule compares the relays with the lowest matched group, so extra groups can only make the relays look less special, never more. Left eye: outside the stimulated looming neurons, the brain fired 13,581-14,040 spikes with a matched group silenced, against 13,901-14,760 with the relays silenced and 14,502-15,172 with nothing silenced. One model, brain only, one stimulus strength (80 spikes/s), 5 matched groups on the left eye only, each run once; the 5 groups all share the same three most active neurons, so they are not independent draws; not a real fly.

Our looming test at 30 spikes/s (21 Oct 2026, pre-registered; brain model, then one body run): 21 Oct: we repeated the matched test with a second, independent draw of the same input on the same scrambled brains (one 1-second trial each). On the left side, both scrambled brains matched again, and neither sent a turn command. On the right side, both scrambled brains matched again, and neither sent a turn command. Matching the number of spikes still did not match the pattern: 1,256 to 2,741 neurons fired in the matched scrambled brains, against 427 (left) and 446 (right) in the real brain with this input. With this input the real brain's turn signal on the right side was 6 spikes/s against our threshold of 5, so the real brain itself sits close to our turn rule at this stimulus strength. Walked in the body, the matched scrambled brain with a small steering signal changed the fly's heading by about 1.3 degrees away from the shadow compared with no brain input, under our 10-degree turn rule; the real brain, with the same input, turned it away by about 9.2 degrees (one run each). With this input the real brain's own turn was also under our 10-degree rule. This body run turns the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping; it is not a separate test of the wiring. With a second input draw, the matched scrambled brains again sent no turn command (2 input draws on the same 4 scrambled brains).

Scrambled brains at 30 spikes/s (17 Oct 2026, our own test, pre-registered, brain only): 17 Oct: at 30 spikes/s, the weakest tested input at which the real brain's turn command appeared, we also ran 2 scrambled brains per side (each neuron keeps its number of connections; one 1-second trial each, with the same trial seed as the real-wiring body runs). On the left side, neither scrambled brain sent a turn command, and their steering signals were identical to having no brain, so in the body they walk like the no-brain fly (the real wiring turned it about 11 deg). On the right side, neither scrambled brain sent a turn command, and their steering signals were identical to having no brain, so in the body they walk like the no-brain fly (the real wiring turned it about 17 deg). As at 80 spikes/s, none of the scrambled brains we ran produced the turn; at 30 spikes/s we did not turn their activity up to match the real brain. The scrambled brains were not matched for overall activity: they fired 48% (left) and 44% (right) as many spikes as the real brain at this strength. Most of those spikes were the stimulated input neurons themselves; outside the input, the scrambled brains fired about 1% as many spikes as the real brain. These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring. We ran scrambled brains at 30 and 80 spikes/s, not at 20, 40 or 60.

Relay update under the 13 Oct headline, which stays (17 Oct 2026; a count from the map, not a new trial): "The two sides disagree: on one side silencing the relays lowered the turn neuron's rate more than matched activity elsewhere, on the other it did not. We do not draw a conclusion." We also looked for a stricter control: other active inputs that excite the turn neuron with a similar firing rate and a similar number of connections onto it. In this model there are none for any of the active relay neurons on either side (count of 15 Oct: the busiest relay, PVLP141, fires about 100 spikes/s; no other such input fires above 43), so that stricter test cannot be built here.
